title: International Proceedings: Audit Against Arbitrariness
subtitle: Where the case stands before Serbia, Interpol, the UN and the ECHR.
intro: International institutions are engaged here as independent verification forums. When domestic safeguards are blocked, international oversight remains the final barrier against wrongful conviction.

items.status: Final stage — decision now with the Minister of Justice
items.text: After the Belgrade Court of Appeal confirmed that the conditions for extradition are met, the file passed to the Minister of Justice — the final step in this procedure, with no further avenue of appeal available. At this stage, the minister is obliged to assess the political motivation of the request and humanitarian risks.
items.focus: In practice, Serbian ministers of justice very rarely refuse extradition once the courts have found formal grounds to be satisfied. This is precisely why parallel engagement with international mechanisms is the only realistic means of bringing external scrutiny to bear on this decision.

items.status: 🔄 Under review — CCF confirmed receipt of the complaint
items.text: The defence challenged the Red Notice before the Interpol Commission for the Control of Files (CCF). This is the only body authorised to remove data from the database when the organisation's rules have been violated.
items.focus: The central argument rests on Article 3 of the Interpol Constitution, which prohibits involvement in commercial disputes. The transaction at the heart of the charge has been found lawful by Russian arbitration courts — this is the key evidence of the commercial nature of the case. Furthermore, the Red Notice incorrectly describes Lagovsky as an 'engineer,' while he is an independent lawyer, a status confirmed by contracts and official records.

items.status: Complaint lodged with the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention
items.text: The case has been referred to the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD), a mechanism authorised to determine facts of international law violations during prosecution.
items.focus: The WGAD assesses compliance with Articles 9 and 14 of the ICCPR (right to liberty and fair trial). The central fact: the criminal charge was formulated in secret, without notifying Lagovsky, years after the events took place.

items.text: The ECtHR refused Rule 39 interim measures, which is standard practice for economic cases. However, the full application is being prepared, as Serbia bears full responsibility for the consequences of extradition.
items.focus: The application is built on the risk of violating Article 3 (inhuman treatment), Article 8 (family separation), and the doctrine of 'flagrant denial of justice' (Article 6 ECHR) in Russia. Surrendering a person to a system where access to court is blocked is itself a Convention violation.

items.text: The defence informed the EU Delegation in Serbia of the systemic violations of legality. This submission records that the case is incompatible with the basic rule-of-law standards that underpin Serbia's European integration path.
Lagovsky requested the UNHCR representation in Belgrade for protection against refoulement. The UNHCR has adopted a 'wait-and-see' approach, citing the pending court case.
items.focus: The Serbian asylum procedure has been purely formalistic: the authorities refuse to examine the defense's arguments on their merits. The Administrative Court remains the final domestic instance. Cases of this profile have rarely succeeded at this stage in the past, necessitating particular attention from the UNHCR.

summary: The international dimension provides an external audit of the case. Different institutions examine different aspects: legality of the search (Interpol), arbitrariness of the prosecution (UN), Serbia's Convention responsibility (ECHR), and compliance with Rule of Law standards (EU).
